one_liner: C++23 consteval perfect-hash map/set for fixed keys; ~1.6-1.8x faster string_view hits than std::unordered_map in the author's benchmark.
what_it_does: icy builds an immutable hash map or set from a compile-time list of keys inside a consteval function. Keys can be integers or char-sequence types such as std::string_view. There is no runtime construction, and lookups also work inside static_assert. You write `constexpr auto m = icy::map<std::string_view, int, 3>::make({...});`, where N must equal the list length. After that, find()/contains()/begin()/end()/size() read like std::unordered_map. It is not a drop-in: keys and values are both frozen, there is no operator[]/at()/count(), and iteration follows initializer order.
how_it_is_fast: Construction runs a CHD-style (compress-hash-displace) search, named chd_result/build_perfect_hash in the code. Keys are split into buckets, buckets are placed largest-first, and each bucket gets a displacement seed (up to 4096 tries under up to 128 global seeds) that moves its keys into empty slots. A lookup is one hash, one bucket-slot read and at most one more slot read, with no chains or probe loops. String keys use a constexpr wyhash port, and each slot stores the key's 64-bit hash, so most misses are rejected without touching the key; ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP skips the key compare entirely. Integer keys hash by identity plus multiply-shift (Fibonacci hashing) into deliberately sparse tables, and icy::set keeps the key inside the slot to avoid a second array access.
when_to_use: A fixed set of string keywords, commands or enum names (tens to about 1000 keys) is looked up on a hot path where you would otherwise use a `static const std::unordered_map<std::string_view, T>`.
You are replacing a static std::map/std::set used only for lookup: the author measured 13.6 vs 3.07 ticks/op at 16 string keys and 44.4 vs 3.23 at 1024.
You need lookups inside constant expressions (for example `static_assert(keywords.contains("if"))`) or want no runtime initialization and no static-initialization-order problems.
You want a bounded per-lookup cost: every find() reads at most two table slots, whatever the key set looks like.
The codebase is already on C++23, preferably Clang, which is the toolchain the author's Makefile uses.
when_not_to_use: Keys are not known at compile time, or you need insert/erase or to change mapped values: both keys and values are immutable.
int64-key maps: the author's own data shows only 1.02-1.25x over std::unordered_map, and tsl::robin_set beats icy::set at N=512 (0.673 vs 0.777). Integer tables also use 4-32x N slots.
String lookups on untrusted input with ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP enabled, because a hash-only match can report a false hit. With the macro off, which is the safe mode, the speedup has not been measured.
Pre-C++23 code, or key sets well above about 1000: compile time and constexpr step limits become the constraint.

Code that needs a mature dependency: the repo was created 2026-09-11, is at v0.2.0 with 0 stars and one author, and CI has built and run no tests since the v0.2 rewrite ('ninja: no work to do', 'No tests were found!!!').

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only; the benchmarks use the Tessil robin-map git submodule)
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (`if consteval`, constexpr std::vector and std::sort during consteval construction). The CI matrix names GCC 14, Clang 18, AppleClang (macos-14) and MSVC 2022, but it last compiled tests on v0.1 (2026-09-12). GCC 13 and Clang 17 were dropped from CI. Large key sets need raised constexpr limits (Clang -fconstexpr-steps, GCC -fconstexpr-ops-limit).
integration.platforms: Any target with a C++23 compiler; no SIMD or intrinsics are needed (the 64x64 multiply uses __uint128_t, _umul128 on MSVC x64, or a portable fallback). The v0.2.0 benchmarks ran only on an Apple M4 Max.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The object is immutable after consteval construction and every member function is const noexcept, so concurrent reads need no locking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — read-only find()/contains()/iteration match std::unordered_map/set usage, but construction goes through consteval make() with N in the type, keys and values are immutable, there is no operator[]/at()/count(), no custom hash or equality template parameters, no ordered queries, and iteration is in initializer order, not std::map's sorted order

gotchas: The README's own usage example defines ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP. With it, string-key find() returns a hit when only the 64-bit hash matches, so a non-member key that collides returns the wrong entry. wyhash runs with a fixed public secret and seed 0. The exhaustive tests only check sequential and generated misses against 64 keys. Integer keys always get a full compare.

The macro changes the body of inline member functions. Set it project-wide as a compiler flag, not with a #define in some files, or different translation units get different definitions (an ODR violation).

The build search runs entirely in the constant evaluator. Hundreds of keys can exceed the default constexpr step budgets, and a failed search is a compile error ('could not build a perfect hash within ICY_MAX_BUILDING_ROUNDS rounds'). Raise ICY_MAX_BUILDING_ROUNDS or the compiler's step limit.

Some README text is stale or broken. It says 'table_size == 2 * N ... linear probing', but the code uses hash-and-displace and sizes integer tables at next_pow2(16N+1) up to 64 keys and next_pow2(4N+1) above, so an int64 set of 1024 keys has 8192 16-byte slots (128 KiB), and sets also store every key twice. The CMake bench recipe points at a missing bench.cpp, and tests/CMakeLists.txt passes an undefined ${bench_name}, so the Makefile (Clang-only flags) is the working build path.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick icy over frozen only if you are on C++23, want the lowest per-hit cost on string_view keys, and can accept an experimental one-author project. frozen (C++14, stable, in maintenance mode, also offers ordered sets/maps and a constinit map with mutable values) remains the safer default. Pick it over Kronuz constexpr-phf when you need string keys or stored values, since that library handles integer keys only; icy has no head-to-head benchmark against any sibling (including ConstexprCore/perfect_hash's 1.08 billion queries/s claim).
verified_claims_summary: The author ran an all-hit microbenchmark on an Apple M4 Max (compiler and stdlib unstated; -O3 -march=native; the timer counts CNTVCT_EL0 ticks, not core cycles, so only the ratios mean anything). With hash-only matching (ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP), string_view find() over 16-1024 keys took 2.8-3.2 ticks/op, against 4.9-5.3 for std::unordered_map/set (1.64-1.77x) and 13-44 for std::map/set (up to ~14.9x). int64 find gained only 1.02-1.25x (map) and 1.36-2.39x (set) over std::unordered_*.
status_note: Active but brand-new (created 2026-09-11, v0.2.0 and last commit 2026-09-16, 0 stars, one author). The BSD-3-Clause single header is easy to vendor but should be treated as experimental.
